content: The PCDH11Y gene is a genetic element found exclusively in human males. It encodes a protein called Protocadherin 11Y, which plays a critical role in guiding the development of nerve cells. In contrast, PCDH11X, located on the X chromosome, is present in both sexes and is shared by humans and our closest evolutionary relatives, chimpanzees. However, PCDH11Y, located on the Y chromosome, is unique to males. From an evolutionary perspective, it is estimated that the PCDH11X gene jumped from the X chromosome to the Y chromosome approximately three million years ago. This event coincided with significant evolutionary milestones, such as the increase in human brain size and the first documented use of tools. Furthermore, around 120,000 to 200,000 years ago, the PCDH11Y gene underwent additional transformation, splitting into two parts and reversing its orientation. Both PCDH11X and PCDH11Y belong to the cadherin family of genes. These genes produce proteins that are involved in cellular signaling and are attached to the surface of nerve cells. Interestingly, PCDH11X and PCDH11Y respond differently to retinoic acid, a chemical that plays a crucial role in embryonic development. Retinoic acid stimulates the activity of PCDH11Y but suppresses the activity of PCDH11X. This differential response is thought to contribute to some of the structural and functional differences observed between male and female brains. Professor Tim Crow, a psychiatrist, has proposed that the PCDH11Y gene may also explain the phenomenon of brain lateralization. Humans exhibit lateralized brains, where the two hemispheres become specialized for specific functions. For example, approximately 90% of people use their right hand for tasks requiring fine motor skills. In contrast, chimpanzees do not show a strong preference for one hand over the other. Brain lateralization also explains why, in right-handed individuals, linguistic functions are predominantly localized to the left hemisphere of the brain.
